lesson.title: React useEffect Hook: Dependencies, Event Listeners and Cleanup
lesson.goal: learn the React useEffect hook: run side effects on mount and on state changes, and clean them up

sources.title: React useEffect Hook: Dependencies, Event Listeners and Cleanup

steps.title: Build a counter component
steps.instructions:
Run `npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react`, `cd my-app`, `npm install`, `npm run dev`, then create src/MyComponent.jsx (rendered from App.jsx) with `const [count, setCount] = useState(0)`, a

Count: {count}

and an Add button calling `addCount`, which runs `setCount(c => c + 1)`.

targets.caption: count state variable starting at 0
handler that adds one using the previous state
rendered counter with Add button

explanations.topic: useEffect must be imported from React alongside useState
Creating a state variable and setter with useState
Updater function: take previous state and add one

hints: Start by importing both hooks from 'react': import React, { useState, useEffect } from 'react'.

Declare state with array destructuring: const [count, setCount] = useState(0); then show it in a

as Count: {count}.
Give the button onClick={addCount} (no parentheses) and define function addCount() { setCount(c => c + 1); }.
Make sure App.jsx imports MyComponent and renders <MyComponent />, and that npm run dev shows a Local: URL.
common_mistakes: Writing onClick={addCount()} which calls the function on every render instead of on click.
Forgetting to export MyComponent or to render <MyComponent /> in App.jsx, so nothing appears.
Importing useEffect from the wrong place or misspelling it (useEffects), causing an import error.
Using setCount(count + 1) instead of the updater form c => c + 1 shown in the video.
Returning two sibling elements without a wrapping fragment or div, causing a JSX syntax error.

steps.title: Update title on every render
steps.instructions: Inside MyComponent, call `useEffect(() => { document.title = `Count: ${count}`; });` with no second argument. Click Add and watch the tab title update.

targets.caption: useEffect with only a function, no dependency array
Side effect: update the tab title from count

explanations.topic: useEffect runs side code every time the component re-renders
useEffect takes two arguments: a function and an array of dependencies
Omitting the dependency array runs the effect after every render
The effect also runs initially when the component mounts

hints: Make sure useEffect is imported from 'react' alongside useState.
Call useEffect near the top of your component, after your useState declarations, and pass it an arrow function.
Inside the arrow function, assign a template string to document.title, e.g. `Count: ${count}`.
Don't pass a second argument yet: useEffect(() => { document.title = `Count: ${count}`; });
common_mistakes: Forgetting to import useEffect, causing 'useEffect is not defined'.
Using regular quotes instead of backticks, so the title shows the literal text ${count}.
Passing an empty array [] as a second argument, which makes the title update only on mount.
Calling useEffect inside the click handler or a condition instead of at the top level of the component.
Writing document.title(...) as a function call instead of assigning to it.

steps.title: Run effect only on mount
steps.instructions: Pass an empty dependency array as the second argument to useEffect, e.g. `useEffect(() => { document.title = 'My Counter Program'; }, []);`. Note that the title updates once on mount and not on later clicks, then revert the effect to set the title to the count.

targets.caption: Add [] as the second argument to useEffect
The title is set once, on mount

explanations.topic: An empty dependency array runs the effect only on mount
The title updates once and not on later clicks
Use cases for one-time effects, such as a static page title
Why skipping [] causes needless updates on every re-render

hints: useEffect takes a second argument after the callback function.
Pass an empty array, [], as that second argument so the effect runs only when the component mounts.
Write useEffect(() => { document.title = 'My Counter Program'; }, []); then click Add and watch the tab title. It shouldn't change.
Afterward, revert to the version that sets the title to the count, as the video does at 05:48.
common_mistakes: Putting the [] inside the arrow function body instead of passing it as useEffect's second argument.
Using `${count}` in the title with [] and expecting it to keep updating. With an empty array it shows only the initial count.
Passing an empty object {} or null instead of an empty array [].
Forgetting to import useEffect from 'react'.

steps.title: Depend on count, add subtract
steps.instructions: In src/MyComponent.jsx set the effect's dependency array to [count] so it runs on mount and whenever count changes. Add a Subtract button that calls subtractCount, which runs setCount(c => c - 1).

targets.caption: The dependency array now lists count: the effect runs on mount and whenever count changes.
A copy of addCount that subtracts one from the previous count.
The new Subtract button. The tab title updates on both add and subtract.

explanations.topic: A value in the dependency array runs the effect on mount and when that value changes
No dependency array vs [count]: re-running on unrelated re-renders
Any change to count, up or down, triggers the side effect

hints: Put the state variable that the effect reads inside the empty array you passed to useEffect.
The second argument to useEffect should be [count].
Copy your addCount function, rename it to subtractCount and change + 1 to - 1, using the updater form c => c - 1.
Add a second <button> with onClick={subtractCount} and the text Subtract.
common_mistakes: Leaving the dependency array empty, so the title only updates once on mount.
Writing onClick={subtractCount()}, which calls the function during render and causes a render loop.
Using setCount(count - 1) instead of the updater function c => c - 1.
Putting the dependency array inside the arrow function body instead of passing it as the second argument to useEffect.
Forgetting to rename the copied function, which leaves two addCount declarations.

steps.title: Add color as second dependency
steps.instructions: Add `const [color, setColor] = useState('green')`, a Change Color button whose `changeColor` handler runs `setColor(c => c === 'green' ? 'red' : 'green')`, and give the count paragraph `style={{color: color}}`. Include color in the title (`Count: ${count} ${color}`) and set the dependency array to `[count, color]`.

targets.caption: New color state variable, starting at green
Handler that flips the color using the previous state
Dependency array now lists count and color
New button that toggles the paragraph color

explanations.topic: Updater function: use the previous state of color in a ternary to toggle between red and green
style attribute needs a JavaScript object inside JSX, hence the double curly braces
Without color in the dependency array, the title ignores color changes
Dependency array: the effect re-runs whenever any listed value changes

hints: Add a second state variable for color, starting at "green", and a button with an onClick that calls a changeColor function.
In changeColor, call setColor with an updater: c => c === "green" ? "red" : "green".
Give the count paragraph style={{color: color}}. The outer braces embed JavaScript and the inner braces make the object.
Put color in the title template, then change the dependency array to [count, color] so color changes also update the title.
common_mistakes: Adding color to the title but leaving the dependency array as [count], so the title doesn't change when you click Change color.
Writing style={color: color} with single braces, or passing a string like style="color: red".
Using onClick={changeColor()}, which calls the function during render and causes an infinite re-render loop.
Using = instead of === in the ternary, or misspelling 'green' so the toggle never flips back.

Forgetting the
and having the buttons render on the same line. This is harmless, but it differs from the video.

steps.title: Track window size naively
steps.instructions: Create width and height state initialised from `window.innerWidth` and `window.innerHeight`, render them in paragraphs with a px unit, and write a `handleResize` function that calls `setWidth(window.innerWidth)` and `setHeight(window.innerHeight)`. In the component body, call `window.addEventListener('resize', handleResize)` and `console.log('EVENT LISTENER ADDED')`, then resize the window and see the listeners pile up in the console.

targets.caption: Updates width and height state from the window
Listener added in the component body, so it runs on every render
Width and height rendered with a px unit

explanations.topic: Initial state read from window.innerWidth/innerHeight
Displayed size doesn't change without a resize listener
Adding the listener directly in the component body (no useEffect)
Every re-render adds another listener, so they pile up

hints: Create two pieces of state with useState, one for width and one for height, starting from the window's current inner size.

Render each value in a

with "px" after the variable, e.g. {width}px.
handleResize takes no parameters. It calls setWidth(window.innerWidth) and setHeight(window.innerHeight). Check that the H in setHeight is capitalised.
In the component body (not inside useEffect), call window.addEventListener('resize', handleResize) and console.log('EVENT LISTENER ADDED'). Then resize the window and open DevTools > Console.
common_mistakes: Calling handleResize() when passing it to addEventListener instead of passing the function reference.
Lowercase 'setheight' instead of 'setHeight', which causes a ReferenceError.
Using window.width or window.outerWidth instead of window.innerWidth.
Forgetting to import useState from 'react'.
Using the event name 'onresize' or 'Resize' instead of 'resize'.
Thinking the step is broken because many logs appear. The pile-up of listeners is the intended demonstration.

steps.title: Add listener once in useEffect
steps.instructions: Move the addEventListener call and its console.log into `useEffect(() => { ... }, [])` so they run only when the component mounts. Resize the window and confirm in the console that the listener is added only once (or twice in StrictMode).

targets.caption: Wrap addEventListener in useEffect
Empty array: run only on mount
Watch how many times the log appears

explanations.topic: useEffect takes a function and a dependency array
Empty dependency array means run only on mount
StrictMode runs effects twice in development (setup, cleanup, setup)
Only one listener is needed instead of thousands

hints: Move the addEventListener line and its console.log out of the component body and into a useEffect callback.
useEffect needs two arguments: an arrow function and a dependency array.
To run only on mount, pass an empty array: useEffect(() => { ... }, []);
Seeing the log twice is normal with StrictMode. It should not keep growing as you resize.
common_mistakes: Leaving the original addEventListener call in the component body as well, so listeners still pile up on every render.
Omitting the dependency array entirely, which makes the effect run after every render.
Calling the handler (handleResize()) instead of passing it (handleResize) to addEventListener.
Forgetting to import useEffect from 'react'.
Thinking two console logs mean a bug, when React StrictMode double-invokes effects in development.

steps.title: Return a cleanup function
steps.instructions: Inside the effect, return `() => { window.removeEventListener('resize', handleResize); console.log('EVENT LISTENER REMOVED'); }`. Refresh and check the console for the StrictMode add, remove and add sequence.

targets.caption: The cleanup function returned from useEffect removes the resize listener
StrictMode runs the effect, cleans it up, then runs it again

explanations.topic: Returning a function from useEffect for cleanup
Cleanup runs before the next re-render or on unmount
Why remove listeners: avoid unexpected behavior and free resources
StrictMode runs the effect, cleans up, then runs it again

hints: useEffect can return a function, and React calls it to clean up the effect.
Inside the effect, after addEventListener, add: return () => { ... }.
In the returned function call window.removeEventListener('resize', handleResize), using the same handler reference you added.
Add console.log('EVENT LISTENER REMOVED') in the cleanup, then refresh and open DevTools > Console: you should see added, removed, added.
common_mistakes: Calling removeEventListener directly in the effect body instead of inside the returned function
Passing a new inline arrow function to removeEventListener instead of the same handleResize reference
Misspelling the event name (e.g. 'resized') so it doesn't match the one passed to addEventListener
Placing the return statement outside the useEffect callback, or removing the [] dependency array
Thinking the add/remove/add sequence is a bug when it is just StrictMode in development

steps.title: Add a second useEffect hook
steps.instructions: Add another `useEffect(() => { document.title = `Size: ${width} x ${height}`; }, [width, height]);`. Resize the window and watch the tab title track the size.

targets.caption: The second useEffect sets the tab title to the window size
The dependency array re-runs the effect whenever the size changes

explanations.topic: A component can have more than one useEffect hook
Dependency array [width, height] runs the effect on mount and on every size change
On mount the title shows the size right away, then tracks resizing

hints: Write a separate useEffect below the first one. Don't put this code inside the resize effect.
Inside it, assign document.title using a template string that includes width and height.
Pass [width, height] as the second argument so the effect re-runs when either value changes.
The full code is: useEffect(() => { document.title = `Size: ${width} x ${height}`; }, [width, height]);
common_mistakes: Using quotes instead of backticks, so ${width} shows up literally in the title.
Leaving out the dependency array, so the title updates on every render instead of only on size changes.
Using an empty array [], so the title is set only once on mount and never updates while resizing.
Putting this code inside the first effect's cleanup return instead of in its own useEffect.
